answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: c. 460 – c. 370 BC · Greek physician of Kos
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The sentence is Epidemics, Book I, section XI, in W. H. S. Jones’s Loeb Classical Library translation (first printed 1923), where it reads “As to diseases, make a habit of two things—to help, or at least to do no harm.” What remains genuinely open is not the text but the hand: scholars cannot establish which treatises in the Hippocratic Corpus Hippocrates personally wrote.

source.heading: The source, on the page

docMeta.dd: W. H. S. Jones, Loeb Classical Library, first printed 1923
ἀσκεῖν περὶ τὰ νοσήματα δύο, ὠφελεῖν ἢ μὴ βλάπτειν

source.excerpt: Declare the past, diagnose the present, foretell the future; practise these acts. As to diseases, make a habit of two things—to help, or at least to do no harm. The art has three factors, the disease, the patient, the physician. The physician is the servant of the art. The patient must co-operate with the physician in combating the disease.
trail: Started at Wikiquote ↗, which lists the line in its sourced section with the Greek ἀσκεῖν περὶ τὰ νοσήματα δύο, ὅφελεῖν ἂ μὴ βλάπτειν and a citation to Epidemics, Book I — a pointer, not yet proof.

Went to the translation itself. The full scanned text of Loeb Hippocrates vol. 1 ↗ carries the English sentence on p. 165 and the matching Greek on p. 164, inside section XI. The same scan’s title-page verso reads “First printed 1923.”

Checked the older English for comparison: Francis Adams’s translation ↗ renders the same passage as “to do good or to do no harm” at Section II, subsection 5 — confirming the sentence, and explaining why citations for it disagree on numbering.

Ran the misattribution the other way. Quote Investigator has no article on this line, and Wikipedia’s Hippocratic Oath article ↗ confirms the “first, do no harm” formula is absent from the Oath — which is where nearly everyone files this quote.
source.excerptNote: Read directly from the scanned Loeb text. Note one small drift in circulation: popular renderings insert an extra comma — “or at least, to do no harm” — where Jones’s printed text has none. The words themselves are unchanged.

source.rightsNote: The Greek original is an ancient text, long out of copyright. The English wording quoted here is W. H. S. Jones’s Loeb Classical Library translation, whose title page verso records “First printed 1923” — comfortably before the 1931 US public-domain cutoff, so the translation is public domain too. A modern translation of the same Greek would not be.

author.name: Hippocrates
author.heading: Hippocrates of Kos
author.metaLine: c. 460 – c. 370 BC · Greek physician of Kos, the ‘Father of Medicine’
author.bio: Hippocrates was a physician and philosopher of the Greek classical period, born on the island of Kos around 460 BC and traditionally called the Father of Medicine for insisting that disease had natural rather than divine causes. His name is attached to the Hippocratic Corpus, some sixty treatises on diagnosis, prognosis, ethics and clinical observation. Wikipedia is blunt that the collection “could not have been written by one person” — scholars count roughly nineteen hands in it — so Epidemics is Hippocratic in the sense that matters bibliographically, while personal authorship stays unresolved.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: The wording is authentic, so the errors here are about where it comes from and who put the pen to it — both of which the internet gets wrong with impressive consistency.

items.why: This is the big one. The sentence is from Epidemics, a book of clinical case records, not from the Oath. Wikipedia’s article on the Oath states that no phrase from which ‘First’ or ‘Primum’ can be translated appears in the text of the original oath ↗. The Oath’s own harm clause promises to abstain from “all intentional wrong-doing and harm.”

The Latin motto is not ancient. Wikipedia’s account ↗ reports that Worthington Hooker introduced it to British and American medicine in Physician and Patient (1847), crediting the Parisian pathologist Auguste François Chomel, and that Cedric M. Smith traced the expression to an attribution to Thomas Sydenham in Thomas Inman’s book of 1860.

The line is securely in the Hippocratic Corpus; whose hand wrote it is another matter. Wikipedia ↗ notes that the question of whether Hippocrates authored any treatise in the corpus “has not been conclusively answered,” and that the collection could not have been written by one person.

misattribution.truthLine: The real thing is a working clause inside Epidemics, Book I — “Declare the past, diagnose the present, foretell the future; practise these acts. As to diseases, make a habit of two things—to help, or at least to do no harm” — readable on page 165 of Jones’s Loeb translation ↗.

context.heading: Why this sentence keeps getting rewritten
lead: Almost everyone who reaches for “first, do no harm” is reaching for this sentence and missing it. The maxim they half-remember is not in the Hippocratic Oath — Wikipedia’s article on the Oath says so flatly, noting that no phrase from which ‘First’ or ‘Primum’ can be translated appears in the text of the original oath ↗. The Oath’s actual harm clause is narrower and more practical: in Jones’s translation the physician swears to use treatment to help the sick “but never with a view to injury and wrong-doing.”

The sentence people actually want sits in a different book entirely, buried in a passage of clinical housekeeping about reading the signs of a crisis. It arrives without ceremony, one clause among several: declare the past, diagnose the present, foretell the future — and, as to diseases, help or at least do no harm. It is advice on how to behave when you do not know what else to do, which is why it has outlived nearly everything around it.
detailsBody: Different English editions cut Epidemics Book I differently, which is why citations for this line disagree. The Loeb edition places it in section XI. Francis Adams’s older translation, hosted at MIT’s Internet Classics Archive ↗, puts the same passage at Section II, subsection 5 — and renders it far less memorably, as the physician having “two special objects in view with regard to disease, namely, to do good or to do no harm.” Wikiquote cites it as Book I, Ch. 2.

The modern popularity of the crisper wording is a translation effect, not a textual one. Adams’s “to do good or to do no harm” is the version Wikipedia quotes when discussing the maxim’s ancestry; Jones’s “to help, or at least to do no harm” is the version that circulates as a quotation. Same Greek, same sentence, different century of English.
context.pull: The line everyone quotes as the Oath’s opening promise is a working note from a book of case records.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "As to diseases, make a habit of two things — to help, or at least, to do no harm" in its sourced section, cited to Epidemics Book I, with the Greek ἀσκεῖν περὶ τὰ νοσήματα δύο, ὠφελεῖν ἢ μὴ βλάπτειν.

The Loeb Classical Library translation by W. H. S. Jones contains, on p. 165, "Declare the past, diagnose the present, foretell the future; practise these acts. As to diseases, make a habit of two things—to help, or at least to do no harm." with the facing Greek on p. 164 in section XI; the title page verso reads "First printed 1923". The same volume's Oath reads "I will abstain from all intentional wrong-doing and harm" and contains no "first, do no harm".
The Internet Archive item record for Loeb Hippocrates volume 1 names W. H. S. Jones (1876–1963) as translator and Heinemann as publisher, in a bilingual Greek/English Loeb edition.

Francis Adams's translation of Of the Epidemics, Book I, renders the same passage at Section II, subsection 5 as the physician having "two special objects in view with regard to disease, namely, to do good or to do no harm", alongside "The physician is the servant of the art".

The phrase "primum non nocere" does not appear in early versions of the Hippocratic Oath; Worthington Hooker introduced the Latin axiom to American and British medicine in Physician and Patient (1847), crediting Auguste François Chomel; Cedric M. Smith traced the expression to an attribution to Thomas Sydenham in Thomas Inman's 1860 book.

Wikipedia states that although "First do no harm" is often said to be part of the original Hippocratic Oath, no phrase from which "First" or "Primum" can be translated appears in the text of the original oath, and quotes the Jones translation's actual harm clause.

Hippocrates is dated c. 460 – c. 370 BC, born on Kos, a physician and philosopher called the Father of Medicine; whether he authored any treatise in the Hippocratic Corpus "has not been conclusively answered", and the corpus could not have been written by one person.
